findings.headline: Substantive audit procedures to verify financial statements are deferred to 2025/26, leaving the council without current audited accounts
findings.detail: All substantive testing procedures (estimated at £25,000–£30,000, plus £32,000 for risk assessment, funded by MHCLG) are scheduled to be completed during the 2025/26 audit year. This deferral means the council cannot provide audited financial statements to verify accounts for 2023/24 and 2024/25 within normal timeframes.
findings.matters: Lenders typically require current audited accounts to verify financial stability and borrowing capacity. Extended deferral of substantive procedures means the council cannot demonstrate its actual financial position or available borrowing headroom to prospective lenders.
findings.figures: £32,000 risk assessment; £25,000–£30,000 estimated substantive work; all procedures scheduled for 2025/26 audit year
findings.quote: We note our fees for this work are expected to be in region of: - Risk assessment - £32,000 (Agreed with management and reported within our ISA260 for the year ended 31 March 2025 but still subject to agreement with PSAA) - Substantive work – We have estimated a cost between £25,000 - £30,000.

findings.headline: South Holland has received disclaimer of opinion from auditors for three consecutive financial years: 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25
findings.detail: The council's predecessor auditor disclaimed opinion for 2022/23. The current auditor (KPMG) disclaimed opinion for 2023/24 on 13 February 2025 and for 2024/25 on 24 February 2026, both issued to meet statutory backstop dates set by government measures to address the local government audit backlog.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years without audited financial statements means the council cannot demonstrate the accuracy of its financial position, reserves, or borrowing capacity to lenders—critical information for any lending decision.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: For the Council this had the impact of a disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for one financial year up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 13 February to comply with the statutory backstop date. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimer of opinion on 24 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
findings.headline: Joint working between Council and PSPS lacks clear governance and remains a key risk area
findings.detail: Audit found lack of clarity and consistency in how services are governed and controlled across Council and PSPS joint working arrangements. This is identified as a key risk area requiring continued management focus, with lower assurance assignments highlighting weaknesses in defined roles, responsibilities and oversight.
findings.matters: Unclear roles and responsibilities in shared service arrangements can lead to gaps in oversight, duplicated effort, or services not being managed according to the council's standards.
findings.figures: One limited assurance assignment, other lower assurance assignments identified weaknesses
findings.quote: lack of clarity and consistency in how services are governed and controlled. Audit work undertaken during 2025/26 identified that this remained a key risk area requiring continued management focus

findings.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
findings.headline: Audit recommendations not being implemented within agreed timescales
findings.detail: Management has not embedded previous years' agreed actions despite past implementation dates. Progress reports continue to track overdue management actions. This indicates improvements to the control environment are not being delivered at adequate pace.
findings.matters: If management is not urgently implementing audit-agreed fixes, the control gaps identified will persist, extending the period of elevated risk.
findings.figures: Actions from 2025 audit remained incomplete and not embedded
findings.quote: Actions agreed following the 2025 internal audit remained incomplete and not embedded, despite past implementation dates

findings.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
findings.headline: Overall governance, risk and control framework rated 'limited' — control framework not operating effectively
findings.detail: The head of internal audit concludes that the frameworks are limited and that testing has demonstrated controls are not operating effectively to mitigate key risks. Several key controls are absent or not being applied. The rating reflects one no assurance review, one limited assurance, with the remainder adequate or substantial.
findings.matters: A limited assurance opinion on the entire control framework undermines confidence in financial reporting, budget management, and management's ability to execute plans.
findings.figures: One no assurance, one limited assurance, majority adequate to substantial
findings.quote: the frameworks of governance, risk and internal controls are limited, and audit testing has demonstrated that the control framework is not operating effectively to mitigate key risks

findings.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
findings.headline: Council unable to reliably track and deliver 2026/27 budget savings with residual financial risk
findings.detail: Q1 audit found insufficient controls to test savings monitoring (seven key findings, five root causes). Q4 follow-up showed a new governance process was implemented, but with only limited assurance over its effectiveness. No formally documented escalation process exists for savings proposals falling behind schedule.
findings.matters: If the council cannot reliably identify and track whether savings are on track, there is cash flow risk and potential unplanned service cuts or increased borrowing mid-year.
findings.figures: Seven key findings in Q1 audit; no efficiency targets required in balanced budgets but residual risk remains
findings.quote: residual financial risk remains over delivery of savings until it is fully tested

findings.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund grant received 'no assurance' rating for control failures
findings.detail: Audit found failures in the control environment, safeguards and oversight of the UKSPF grant. The governance framework for the grant lifecycle is described as unclear and inadequate, resulting in weak controls, poor accountability and insufficient oversight. The audit is still at draft stage but a No Assurance rating is anticipated.
findings.matters: A statutory grant with no assured controls creates risk of audit disqualification, requirement to repay funds, or loss of future grant access. This is a direct compliance and cash risk.
findings.figures: One 'no assurance' review at draft stage
findings.quote: the findings reflect an unclear and inadequate governance framework, leading to weak controls, poor accountability, and insufficient oversight across the grant lifecycle, resulting in a 'No Assurance' rating being anticipated

findings.headline: Regulatory compliance committed £150,295 in 2025/26 through three new leadership roles and external support, representing ongoing budget commitment
findings.detail: Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 directed specific activities. Council created Tenant Engagement Lead (£63,355), ASB Lead (£27,209), and Housing Insight/Improvement Lead (£47,489); engaged Altair for compliance support (£12,242). These appear to be ongoing roles, not one-time costs, making them recurring housing budget commitments.
findings.matters: Regulatory-driven staffing costs reduce financial flexibility and compete with service delivery or reserve availability. Lenders assess whether council can absorb compliance spending without financial strain.
findings.quote: Tenant Engagement and Influence Lead Officer £63,355 ASB Lead Officer £27,209 Housing Service Insight and Improvement Lead Officer £47,489 Altair - for support post inspections £12,242 Total Spend for 2025/26 £150,295

findings.headline: South Holland received C2 housing regulation judgment (July 2025) with improvement plan on track but ongoing compliance investment required
findings.detail: Regulator of Social Housing issued C2 grade after inspection (February-July 2025), indicating standards broadly met but weaknesses in Transparency, Influence and Accountability. Council adopted improvement plan November 2025 and is reporting measurable progress across stock condition surveys, tenant engagement, and ASB policies. Regulator has de-escalated engagement from monthly to bi-monthly meetings, signalling confidence in improvement trajectory.
findings.matters: Regulatory judgments on housing are material governance indicators for lenders assessing council resilience and management credibility. C2 is a watchpoint short of crisis, but progress and regulator satisfaction reduce escalation risk.
findings.figures: C2 grade; sector context shows 9 C1, 29 C2, 20 C3, 4 C4 across programmed inspections
findings.quote: Following the inspection of South Holland District Council as a social landlord between February and July 2025, and the subsequent publication of the Regulatory Judgement on 30th July 2025, the Council received a C2 grade. This confirmed that while the Consumer Standards were broadly met, weaknesses required attention

findings.paper_title: SHDC Draft Outturn Covering Report 2025-26 RP
findings.headline: HRA debt restructured in March 2026: £67.456m prematurely repaid and replaced with £50.000m new borrowing
findings.detail: The council made a significant debt management decision in March 2026, prematurely repaying £67.456m of HRA debt and refinancing with £50.000m of new borrowing. This generated a discount of £18.371m, which will be amortised over 10 years, creating an ongoing annual credit of £1.837m to the HRA from 2025/26 onwards. The council states this refinancing is a key driver of the £3.130m HRA underspend for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A lender tracks council debt reduction and refinancing decisions; this shows material reduction in HRA debt, successful refinancing execution, and an ongoing £1.837m annual revenue benefit.
findings.figures: £67.456m debt repaid; £18.371m discount; £50.000m new borrowing; £1.837m annual HRA credit from 2025/26
findings.quote: In March 2026, the Council prematurely repaid its £67.456m of HRA debt, generating a discount of £18.371m and replaced it with £50.000m of new borrowing. This discount will be amortised over 10 years, resulting in an annual credit of £1.837m to the HRA from 2025/26 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix to the Housing Landlord Strategy - root cause analysis
findings.headline: The council has committed to new dedicated resource and budget for tenant engagement implementation from 2026, including a new dedicated role.
findings.detail: In response to the C2 grading, the council has formally budgeted additional spending on tenant engagement. This includes establishment of a dedicated role for tenant engagement leadership and additional capacity to support implementation from 2026 onwards. This represents a shift from project-based activity to long-term operational commitment within the housing service.
findings.matters: New budget commitments for compliance remediation affect the council's financial position and spending plans, and indicate the financial cost of addressing the regulatory finding.
findings.figures: Dedicated resource allocated; new role focused solely on tenant engagement; additional capacity budgeted for 2026
findings.quote: Dedicated resource has been allocated, including a new role focused solely on tenant engagement, and additional capacity has been budgeted to support implementation from 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix to the Housing Landlord Strategy - root cause analysis
findings.headline: Capacity constraints forced the council to defer tenant engagement work in favour of safety, quality and governance compliance in its transformation programme.
findings.detail: The council undertook risk-based prioritization of its transformation programme, placing safety, quality, and governance improvements first due to limited capacity to implement multiple initiatives simultaneously. Tenant engagement, although recognized as important, was scheduled for a later phase to ensure it could be delivered meaningfully and sustainably. This sequencing decision meant that formal, council-wide tenant engagement structures were not in place by the time of the regulatory inspection.
findings.matters: Resource constraints that force difficult prioritization choices indicate limited operational capacity to address multiple compliance and improvement areas simultaneously, which may affect the council's ability to deliver across multiple service areas.
findings.figures: Transformation resources increased October 2024; Housing Transformation Team established December 2023
findings.quote: Capacity constraints and the need to sequence transformation activities meant that foundational compliance and governance work took precedence. Engagement was recognised as important but was scheduled for a later phase to ensure it could be delivered meaningfully and sustainably.

findings.paper_title: Appendix to the Housing Landlord Strategy - root cause analysis
findings.headline: South Holland received a C2 regulatory grading for weakness in the Transparency, Accountability and Influence Standard.
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C2 grading primarily due to the absence of a formal, embedded approach to tenant engagement across the whole tenant cohort. The council had focused engagement efforts only on sheltered housing tenants during a service redesign, rather than across all tenants. While the council had begun developing a Tenant Engagement Strategy with external experts (TPAS) and was undertaking improvement work, these were still in early stages at the time of inspection.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade indicates governance and compliance risk, affects the council's regulatory standing, and may trigger closer ongoing oversight by the housing regulator.
findings.figures: C2 grading; Tenant Engagement Strategy adopted June 2025; Tenant Forum established July 2025
findings.quote: The primary driver behind the C2 grading was due to weaknesses with the Transparency, Accountability and Influence Standard, specifically the absence of a formal, embedded approach to tenant engagement across the whole tenant cohort.

findings.headline: Shared services dependency on PSPS Ltd partnership carries service delivery risk with limited fallback
findings.detail: The council operates 'outsourced services within its TECKAL company, PSPS Ltd' in partnership with Boston Borough and East Lindsey. A risk is identified: 'PSPS may be unable to deliver an effective service within the agreed contract price' (rated Low/Medium). The council states the partnership 'provide a significant opportunity to drive savings, efficiencies, transformation, and improvement' but if this fails, the shared structure offers limited independent recovery options.
findings.matters: Outsourcing core services to a shared company reduces the council's control and creates single-point-of-failure risk. If PSPS cannot deliver within contract price, all three councils are impacted simultaneously, limiting negotiating power and forcing collective renegotiation.
findings.figures: Shared services delivery via PSPS Ltd partnership (3 councils); risk identified as Low/Medium impact for service failure
findings.quote: The Council's new partnership and the outsourced services within its TECKAL company, PSPS Ltd, provide a significant opportunity to drive savings, efficiencies, transformation, and improvement across the 3 Councils.

findings.headline: Efficiency savings requirement of £1.24m (2027/28) identified as 'key challenge requiring political and cultural direction'
findings.detail: The council explicitly recognises that 'the ongoing delivery of efficiencies is recognised as a key challenge to the Council that will require both political and cultural direction to ensure it is met.' Required efficiencies are: £1.239m (2027/28), £927k (2028/29), £632k (2029/30). These follow a balanced 2026/27 with no efficiency target, meaning pressures will suddenly surface.
findings.matters: The council has identified efficiency delivery as difficult and requiring senior political commitment. The sudden jump from zero target in 2026/27 to £1.2m in 2027/28 suggests the council knows significant pressures are being deferred, not solved.
findings.quote: The ongoing delivery of efficiencies is recognised as a key challenge to the Council that will require both political and cultural direction to ensure it is met.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy income falling £2.44m (23%) in single year due to Universal Credit rollout
findings.detail: Housing Benefit Subsidy income is forecast to fall from £10.439m (2025/26) to £7.996m (2026/27), a reduction of £2.443m. This is 'driven by the significant reduction in Housing Benefit Subsidy as caseloads continue to fall' due to Universal Credit rollout. The paper confirms 'a corresponding reduction in expenditure' but this represents a major income stream contraction.
findings.matters: A £2.4m reduction in a non-discretionary income stream (housing benefit subsidy) indicates the council's revenue base is shrinking through policy change beyond its control, requiring service redesign or alternative income.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit Subsidy: £10.439m (2025/26) declining to £7.996m (2026/27); reduction of £2.443m (23%)
findings.quote: Reductions in the Housing Benefit Subsidy income reflect current anticipated levels of activity affected by the rollout of Universal Credit.

findings.headline: HRA regulatory compliance costs rising due to material weakness findings and Awaab's Law implementation
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing identified 'a material weakness in tenant engagement and influence' in July 2025. The council is adding 6 FTE to the HRA establishment (4 converting fixed-term posts, 2 new) specifically to meet regulator expectations and 'support the organisation in achieving a C1 grading.' Additionally, demand for repairs is 'further impacted following the implementation of Awaab's Law' with sector benchmarking indicating 'demand is unlikely to decline.'
findings.matters: Regulatory weakness findings drive mandatory cost increases and staffing additions. Awaab's Law compliance on damp/condensation/mould creates ongoing expenditure pressure with no ceiling. Both represent regulatory risks that will continue to consume resources.
findings.figures: 6 FTE additions to HRA establishment for 2026/27; 2 new posts plus 4 conversions from fixed-term; regulatory judgement from July 2025
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing identified a material weakness in tenant engagement and influence in its July 2025 regulatory judgement. Additional dedicated capacity is essential to meet the Regulator's expectations for establishing scrutiny arrangements, enhanced tenant involvement, and to support the organisation in achieving a C1 grading.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme jumping to £25.35m (2026/27) driven by £13.3m internal borrowing
findings.detail: The general fund capital programme increases from £14.681m (2025/26) to £25.352m (2026/27), a 73% increase. This is predominantly funded by internal borrowing of £13.276m, consuming the council's cash reserves. Treasury assumptions show investment balances declining from £25.4m to £21.2m to £11.8m over three years, indicating cash depletion.
findings.matters: Rapid drawdown of investment balances through capital spending funded by internal borrowing reduces the council's cash liquidity and increases future external borrowing risk. The declining cash position limits financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Programme: £14.681m (2025/26) to £25.352m (2026/27); internal borrowing £13.276m (2026/27); investment balances forecast £25.4m → £21.2m → £11.8m
findings.quote: Increased capital investment in Council assets to help generate new income streams, reduce running costs, and help deliver services more efficiently.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing programme of £31.5m over five years and external borrowing expected September 2026
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme of £70.855m over five years will be funded by £31.522m of external borrowing. The council expects external borrowing of £7m in September 2026 to fund 2026/27 capital, described as 'lower than the £10m budgeted in 2025/26' but still material. This increases interest costs and debt burden.
findings.matters: Increasing HRA borrowing raises debt service costs, reduces financial flexibility, and increases the council's exposure to interest rate risk. The actual £7m borrowing still represents a significant additional debt obligation.
findings.figures: HRA external borrowing: £6.676m (2026/27), £31.522m total over five years (2026/27 to 2030/31); expected September 2026 borrowing £7m
findings.quote: External Borrowing of £7m to fund the HRA 2026/27 Capital programme is expected in September 2026, lower than the £10m budgeted in 2025/26.

findings.headline: HRA General Reserve declining £2.79m in single year to £3.476m, creating tighter financial cushion
findings.detail: The HRA general reserve is forecast to fall from £6.267m (31 March 2026) to £3.476m (31 March 2027), a decline of £2.791m. This reserve funds both revenue and capital, and one-off projects. The council states the Stock Condition Survey (£184k) that was funded from reserves in 2025/26 'will not be financed from there in 2026/27,' indicating reserve depletion for service delivery.
findings.matters: A 44% reduction in HRA reserves in one year reduces the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or service pressures in housing, and indicates increasing reliance on borrowing for HRA capital.
findings.figures: HRA General Reserve: £6.267m (31/3/26) declining to £3.476m (31/3/27); reduction of £2.791m
findings.quote: The Stock Condition Survey £184k was funded from reserves in 2025/26 but will not be financed from there in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Funding protection cliff edge: transitional protection ends in 2029/30, removing £521m annual grant
findings.detail: The council receives 95% protection of income through a transitional funding floor due to anticipated Fair Funding Assessment reduction exceeding 15% by 2028/29. This protection is payable over three years to 2028/29 (£299k in 2027/28, £521k in 2028/29), then 'reduce to Nil from 2029/30 onwards.' The council explicitly states there 'remains a high degree of uncertainty beyond 2028/29.'
findings.matters: A £521k annual loss starting 2029/30 creates a medium-term funding cliff that will require new savings or borrowing decisions if not addressed earlier.
findings.figures: Funding Floor: £299k (2027/28), £521k (2028/29), then nil from 2029/30
findings.quote: South Holland will receive £0.299m in 2027/28 and £0.521m in 2028/29, then reduce to Nil from 2029/30 onwards.

findings.headline: Business Rates Retention system reset reduces council income by £2.97m in a single year
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review has fundamentally reset how business rates are retained. Net retained business rates income falls from £7.152m in 2025/26 to £4.186m in 2026/27. This is the largest single structural change to council funding identified in the settlement and is described as a reduction that is 'significant'.
findings.matters: A £2.97m reduction in recurring income represents a fundamental shift in the council's resource base and requires offsetting through either reserves, borrowing, or service reduction.
findings.figures: Net Retained Business Rates: £7.152m (2025/26) to £4.186m (2026/27); reduction of £2.966m
findings.quote: As a result of the reset of the Business Rates Retention system, from 1st April 2026, as part of Government's Fair Funding Review, the net Retained Business Rates income has reduced significantly from prior years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: MRP policy defers charges on Welland Homes equity using annuity method over 50 years, concentrating cost to later years
findings.detail: The council is charging MRP on its £3.705m Welland Homes share capital using an annuity method (deferred charges) over 50 years at the PWLB annuity rate, not a straight-line method. The guidance notes this method is used 'where the flow of benefits from an asset are expected to increase in later years,' but a housing stock typically has stable benefits, not increasing ones. This defers revenue charges and increases future financial commitments.
findings.matters: Annuity MRP is less conservative and loads costs into the outer years of the forecast, when other commitments may be tighter. For a lender assessing medium-term sustainability, deferred charges mask near-term pressure and concentrate risk.
findings.figures: Share Capital £3.705m; MRP charged on annuity basis over 50 years; 2026/27 MRP charge: £14k
findings.quote: MRP charged on an annuity basis over a 50 year period. The annuity rate used will be the 50 year PWLB rate on 27/02/25. Equity stake in Welland Homes. Underlying assets of the Company is houses with useful life in excess of 50 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Council has £10.25m invested in Welland Homes, a commercial property venture, outside standard treasury rules
findings.detail: The council has issued £6.546m in loans to Welland Homes and holds £3.705m in share capital (equity). These are classified as 'non-treasury investments' and sit outside normal investment limits. Welland Homes loans are being managed through MRP using projected loan repayments rather than statutory provision. The council sought 'independent professional opinion' on the useful life of the underlying housing assets.
findings.matters: A large, illiquid equity stake in a housing company introduces credit risk and liquidity risk. If Welland Homes runs into difficulty, the council has limited recourse. The special MRP treatment (deferring charges to loan repayments) also concentrates cash flow risk in future years.
findings.figures: Loans to Welland Homes: £6.546m at 31 December 2025; Share capital: £3.705m; MRP 2026/27: £14k (only 14k on 3.7m equity)
findings.quote: In addition to the above the Council has issued loans to Welland Homes totalling £6.546m at 31 December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Council maintains £31.9m under-borrowed position, betting on interest rates falling from current 4.81–6.01% PWLB rates
findings.detail: The council is deliberately holding reserves to defer borrowing, wagering that PWLB rates will fall. MUFG forecasts 5-year PWLB rates at 4.81% now, declining to 4.10% by end of 2027. If this forecast is wrong and rates rise instead, the council will face higher borrowing costs and may be forced to borrow at unfavourable rates to meet its capital programme.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasting risk is material. If the council misjudges and rates rise, it incurs avoidable debt service cost increases. The under-borrowing position is not conservative; it is a directional bet on the economy.
findings.figures: Under / (over) borrowing 2026/27: £31,920k; Current PWLB 5-year certainty rate: 4.81%; Target (end Q4 2027): 4.10%
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Capital financing need jumps 414% in a single year, driven by Large Urban Fund projects
findings.detail: Net financing need for the year is forecast to rise from £3.879m in 2025/26 to £19.952m in 2026/27 — a £16m jump in one year. This is primarily driven by Large Urban Fund (LUF) projects increasing from £10.163m to £15.511m. The Council is making a very significant capital commitment that will require substantial borrowing.
findings.matters: A sudden four-fold increase in capital financing need signals major new commitments and associated borrowing. This increases the council's debt service costs and financial risk profile materially.
findings.figures: Net financing need 2025/26: £3.879m; 2026/27: £19.952m; LUF Projects increase from £10.163m to £15.511m
findings.quote: Net financing need for the year 3,879 19,952 6,238 5,216 9,332 5,738

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: HRA debt growing to unsustainable levels against revenue, climbing from 357% to 449% of revenue over five years
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account debt is forecast to grow from £67.5m to £98.5m by 2030/31, while revenues grow from £18.9m to £21.9m. The debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorates from 357% to 449%, and debt per dwelling rises from £17,668 to £26,318. This trajectory is not financially sustainable and represents an accelerating commitment.
findings.matters: For a lender, rising debt-to-revenue ratios are a primary risk indicator. A council where housing debt exceeds revenues by nearly 5x is exposed to service disruption risk and leaves no headroom for income shocks.
findings.figures: HRA debt £m: 67.456 (2025/26) to 98.456 (2030/31); ratio of debt to revenues %: 357 to 449; debt per dwelling £: 17,668 to 26,318
findings.quote: Ratio of debt to revenues % 357 380 394 410 433 449

findings.headline: Treasury function is being relied upon to contribute to revenue budget relief.
findings.detail: The strategy states treasury management 'will be expected to make a positive contribution towards both revenue and capital pressures'. The council holds approximately £35m in average cash holdings and is counting on investment returns to help absorb the revenue budget gap.
findings.matters: Using treasury returns to cover structural budget deficits is unsustainable. Investment returns are volatile and cannot reliably offset growing budget pressures, signalling the council is looking to short-term measures rather than structural solutions.
findings.figures: Surplus cash averages approximately £35m
findings.quote: Treasury management will be expected to make a positive contribution towards both revenue and capital pressures.

findings.headline: Council is planning new borrowing to fund capital investment amid growing revenue pressures.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states the council 'needs to consider ways of innovation that limit the amount of investment required during the timescale of this strategy in light of the significant pressures upon its resources, which will include new borrowing'. This signals intent to borrow for capital purposes.
findings.matters: New borrowing adds debt servicing costs and future Minimum Revenue Provision obligations to a budget already under growing pressure. A lender must assess whether the council can afford repayment.
findings.figures: New borrowing amount unspecified in this strategy
findings.quote: The Council also needs to consider ways of innovation that limit the amount of investment required during the timescale of this strategy in light of the significant pressures upon its resources, which will include new borrowing.

findings.headline: Business rate retention changes create significantly higher risk to a core income stream.
findings.detail: Changes to the localised business rate retention system are flagged as an area of focus, with the council concerned about yield changes from economic impacts and recent government policy. The document explicitly states this income stream now 'has a significantly higher level of risk'.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core council revenue source. Higher risk to this stream directly threatens revenue budget stability and the ability to service new debt.
findings.figures: Risk impact unquantified
findings.quote: so this income stream has a significantly higher level of risk. There are no signs of an upturn in Council or indeed Government finances to provide optimism.

findings.headline: Council holds limited general and specific reserves to weather financial shocks.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it holds 'limited levels' of both general and specific reserves, meaning minimal financial buffers to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls without borrowing.
findings.matters: Limited reserves signal weak financial resilience. A council cannot absorb service pressures or unexpected costs without emergency borrowing, increasing debt and revenue obligations.
findings.figures: Reserves described only as 'limited' (unquantified)
findings.quote: South Holland District Council holds limited levels of both general and specific reserves.

findings.headline: Revenue budget balancing is becoming harder each year through to 2030/31 with no expected improvement.
findings.detail: The council states that 'each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging' through 2030/31, driven by inflationary pressures, reduced post-COVID income, and business rate changes. The document explicitly notes 'there are no signs of an upturn in Council or indeed Government finances to provide optimism', forcing difficult choices between efficiency, income raising, and service reduction.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can sustain balanced budgets. Growing annual challenges indicate deteriorating financial resilience and increased risk of future deficits or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Budget pressures through 2030/31
findings.quote: Each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging, with options ranging from becoming more efficient, raising additional income and/or reducing services.

findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatements of £623k remain in the draft accounts
findings.detail: KPMG identified three misstatements management did not correct: £333k computer licence accrual error (£5k factual + £328k projected), £191k property understatement, and £99k car park valuation error. These would decrease the deficit by £623k if corrected. KPMG formally requests their correction per ISA 450.
findings.matters: While individually immaterial, management chose not to correct identified errors, suggesting either resource constraints or lack of rigour in closure. The pattern (accruals, valuations) indicates control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £623k total uncorrected; £333k licence; £191k PPE; £99k car park
findings.quote: In line with ISA (UK) 450 we request that you correct uncorrected misstatements. However, they will have no effect on the opinion in our auditor's report, individually or in aggregate.

findings.headline: Formal record of decisions on efficiency savings does not exist, yet the Council needs to achieve £1m-£1.8m annual savings
findings.detail: Cabinet meetings held to discuss savings produced a list reviewed by Senior Leadership Team, but no minutes or action logs were kept. Business and Efficiency Savings meetings are not minuted. Internal Audit found insufficient controls in place for identification and monitoring of savings. The approved budget requires £1m savings in 2025/26, rising to £1.8m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Significant savings targets exist but governance over delivery is absent. Without formal tracking or committee oversight, the Council risks missing targets and facing budget deficits, directly affecting debt serviceability and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £1m savings required 2025/26; £1.8m required by 2028/29
findings.quote: We confirmed that a meeting was held with the Cabinet members to discuss savings before the 2024-25 budget was set. A list of potential savings was identified and discussed at this meeting, which was subject to review by the Senior Leadership Team (SLT). We requested evidence of this meeting however no minutes or actions logs have been kept by the Council.

findings.headline: £1.1m of property assets cannot be accurately verified due to missing floor plan data
findings.detail: Of 40 floor areas used in property valuations, 8 (20%) did not have supporting floor plans. Of these, 2 assets totalling £1.1m could not be verified at all. Additionally, 6 other assets had correctable errors totalling £191k in understatement. This weakness was raised in the prior year and not resolved.
findings.matters: Property valuations represent the largest asset on a council balance sheet. Nearly £1.2m cannot be reliably verified, undermining calculations for reserves and debt capacity. The fact this issue persisted from prior year suggests weak management controls.
findings.figures: £1.1m unverifiable; £191k understatement; 8 out of 40 floor areas (20%) unsupported; Other Land and Buildings total £28.06m
findings.quote: We identified that there are 8 out of 40 floor areas used in the valuation that were not supported by adequate floor plans or did not exist. 2 of the 8 we could not verify which have a value of £1.1m

findings.headline: The auditors are disclaiming their opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient evidence over reserves
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. They cite this as pervasive to the Council's financial position. This is a continuation of prior-year disclaimer opinions for 2023/24 and 2022/23.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditors cannot confirm the Council's financial position. For lenders, this means the true asset base, liability position, and debt serviceability cannot be independently verified. This pattern across three years suggests structural audit issues.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 12 February 2025 for 2023/24; disclaimer continuing for 2024/25 due to 27 February 2026 backstop date
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not fully complete and due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Sector-wide financial stress with £2.2bn projected black hole in councils' HRA budgets by 2028, creating macro-level risk context
findings.detail: Over 100 stock-holding councils, including South Holland, have signed the 'securing the future of social housing' campaign raising concerns about HRA financial danger, with £2.2bn projected deficit expected by 2028 nationally.
findings.matters: This shows South Holland is operating within a sector under acute financial stress; any deterioration in council finances or sector-wide factors (rents policy, voids, inflation) could impact this council's position rapidly.
findings.figures: £2.2bn black hole expected by 2028; 100+ councils signed campaign
findings.quote: In 2024, more than 100 stock holding Councils (including South Holland) signed up to the 'securing the future of social housing' campaign raising concerns about the danger of HRA finances, with a £2.2bn black hole in councils' national housing budgets expected by 2028.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: PWLB interest rates have trebled in three years, creating volatile assumptions in a 30-year plan
findings.detail: The business plan is built on current PWLB borrowing rates described as being at 'three times what they were less than 3 years ago'. The plan treats borrowing as 'financing of last resort' but this high-rate environment significantly increases the cost of the £142m new borrowing.
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions are critical to 30-year HRA viability; rates at three-times historical levels mean further rises would materially impact affordability and headroom against the minimum 1.25 ICR threshold.
findings.figures: PWLB rates three times higher than three years ago
findings.quote: Continued high levels of interest rates available from the PWLB (at three times what they were less than 3 years ago)

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard and revised Decent Homes Standard both anticipated for 2026 implementation, driving £3.7m additional cost commitment
findings.detail: Government consultations on MEES and Decent Homes changes are expected to result in implementation during 2026. The council has already committed £3.7m in additional energy efficiency programmes to achieve EPC C rating for all stock by 2030, with these programmes commencing in 2027.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance deadlines are external cost drivers outside the council's control; the 2026 implementation date is imminent and the council's ability to deliver £3.7m of efficiency programmes while managing other pressures will test HRA headroom.
findings.figures: £3.7m additional energy efficiency programmes; EPC C target by 2030
findings.quote: Government consultations on changes to the Decent Homes Standard and the introduction of a Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (MEES) anticipated to be implemented during 2026. Investment into energy efficiency extended to achieve EPC C for all stock by 2030. Additional programmes totalling £3.7m commencing during 2027

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio operating at minimum regulatory threshold of 1.25, leaving tight headroom for unexpected cost increases
findings.detail: The business plan meets the 'golden rule' requirement of an Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25, but operates at this minimum threshold rather than with significant headroom. Any adverse movement in costs or income could breach this requirement.
findings.matters: Operating at minimum regulatory thresholds leaves little buffer for external shocks (interest rate rises, inflation, void rates); lenders typically want to see headroom above minimum requirements.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25
findings.quote: The Plan is fully financed across the 30 years, remaining within the 'golden rule' of an Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25%, so that there is a cushion to ensure interest can be paid in the event of unexpected cost increases.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Management and repair costs at 63p per £1 of rent collected — explicitly above benchmarks for similar councils
findings.detail: The paper identifies that within 2026/27, net costs of management and repairs consume 63p of every £1 of rent income after service charges and non-rent income. The council explicitly states this is 'relatively high compared to benchmarks' and flags it needs efficiency improvements.
findings.matters: Above-benchmark operating costs are a warning sign; the council has acknowledged it and says it will 'keep opportunities to seek greater efficiencies under regular review', but this implies current operations are not yet optimized.
findings.figures: 63p per £1 of rent income
findings.quote: Within 2026/27, net costs of management and repairs (after taking into account service charges and non-rent income) represents 63p of every £1 of rent income collected. We know that this is relatively high compared to benchmarks and will keep opportunities to seek greater efficiencies under regular review

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: £142 million additional borrowing for largest HRA investment programme in council's history
findings.detail: The council plans to invest £235m in housing stock over 30 years, with £142m financed through new borrowing on top of existing £67.5m debt from 2012. The council states this is sustainable based on 30-year assumptions, but represents a material increase in HRA debt levels.
findings.matters: This is a significant borrowing commitment that will increase the council's HRA debt substantially; lenders will want to understand whether the 30-year assumptions (especially rents and inflation) are robust.
findings.figures: £142m new borrowing; £235m total investment; £67.5m existing debt; £257.4m stock valuation
findings.quote: the HRA is projected to generate £854.5m income and invest £235m in the housing stock. This includes £142m financed through borrowing, which factors in the existing £67.5m debt originally taken out in 2012

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account business plan has not been formally updated since 2013/14, and the council is now undertaking an external stock condition survey via Savills to inform long-term HRA financial planning.
findings.detail: The council's long-term HRA business plan was set in 2013/14 (over 11 years ago) and has since been amalgamated only into annual budget setting. In 2024/25, the council engaged Savills PLC to undertake a comprehensive Housing Stock Condition Survey for all council dwellings. The results will form an integral part of the long-term financial plan for the HRA. This indicates the council lacked current data on the condition and long-term maintenance requirements of its housing stock.
findings.matters: The HRA is a ring-fenced account with £14.8m of capital spending and £40.5m of council reserves partly supporting it. A 12-year-old business plan without recent stock condition data creates uncertainty about the true capital maintenance backlog and HRA sustainability. The need for an external review suggests prior planning was deficient.
findings.figures: HRA business plan last formally set 2013/14; HRA capital spend 2024/25 £14.8m; HRA budgeted surplus 2024/25 £669k, actual surplus £194k
findings.quote: The long-term Housing Revenue Account (HRA) business plan was set in 2013/14... The Council engaged Savills PLC, as an external expert, to undertake a review of the Housing Revenue Account stock throughout 2024/25. This information will be utilised for the Council to prepare a long-term financial plan for their HRA.

findings.headline: The Section 151 officer departed in March 2025 during a period when the council's efficiency programme and financial control frameworks are being rebuilt.
findings.detail: The outgoing S151 officer left in March 2025 and had been heavily involved in discussion and updating of the efficiency savings long list. The audit notes that if processes, actions and priorities are not formally documented, there is a risk that key knowledge will be lost, hindering the council's ability to continue to effectively make savings. This departure coincides with internal audit finding insufficient controls in savings identification and monitoring.
findings.matters: The combination of S151 departure and unresolved efficiency programme governance means the council is entering 2025/26 (when it must deliver £1.2m of identified savings) with both new finance leadership and an ineffective savings tracking process.
findings.figures: Departure date March 2025; efficiency requirement 2025/26 £1.2m
findings.quote: The outgoing S151 officer was heavily involved in the discussion and updating of the long list and has left the organisation in March 2025. Therefore, if processes, actions and priorities are not formally documented, there is a risk to the Council that key knowledge will be lost.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery fell significantly short of budget in 2024/25, with general fund capital at 43% and HRA capital at 67% of planned spend.
findings.detail: As at end August 2024 (6 months into the year), the council had spent only £1.6m of an £11m general fund capital budget (15%) and £5.8m of a £22m HRA budget (26%). Despite forecasting a pick-up in the second half, final outturn was £4.8m general fund (43% of budget) and £14.8m HRA (67% of budget). This pattern suggests either project delays or constraints on capital deployment.
findings.matters: Systematic underperformance of capital programmes indicates either project delivery challenges or possible cash constraints. For a council already requiring efficiency savings, the ability to execute planned capital investment is a basic governance measure.
findings.figures: General fund budget £11m, actual £4.8m (43%); HRA budget £22m, actual £14.8m (67%). At Aug 2024: £1.6m of £11m (15%) and £5.8m of £22m (26%) spent
findings.quote: The Council is currently behind their capital programme for General Fund and Housing Revenue Account (HRA). They are reporting capital spend at the end of August 2024 of £1.6m and £5.8m against a full year budget of £11m and £22m respectively.

findings.headline: The Internal Drainage Board levy creates an uncontrolled cost pressure growing at 30% average annually, with limited mitigation beyond annual £335k government support.
findings.detail: The IDB levy is budgeted at £3.4m for 2024/25, up 7.7% from the prior year. Historically the council has seen average increases of 30% between 2021/22 and the current period. The council estimates future increases at 5% per annum. The council received £335k of one-off government support for 2024/25 but is liaising with IDBs and lobbying government for longer-term relief, indicating the pressure is structural and beyond council control.
findings.matters: A cost that grows by 30% on average and represents 4% of the council's gross expenditure (£3.4m against £82m) cannot be offset by service efficiencies alone. This is a demand-driven cost with limited mitigation tools available to the council, creating structural budget risk.
findings.figures: £3.4m 2024/25 (7.7% increase from prior year); historical average increases of 30% from 2021/22; estimated future 5% annual increases; £335k government support 2024/25
findings.quote: The Internal Drainage Board (IDB) levy continues to be a cost pressure for the Council with a budgeted cost of £3.4m in 2024-25 (an increase of 7.7% from 2023/24). The Council has seen increases on average of 30% of the levy from 2021/22.

findings.headline: The formal efficiency programme to deliver £1.8m in annual savings by 2028-29 is not operational and prior-year recommendations have not been implemented.
findings.detail: The council has no formal efficiency programme in place despite identifying this as a medium-risk issue in the prior year audit. The outgoing S151 officer, who left in March 2025, was heavily involved in updating the long list of potential efficiencies, and no formal documentation exists. The council achieved only 62% of its £832k efficiency target in 2024/25. September 2025 internal audit found insufficient controls in the savings identification and monitoring process.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver documented efficiency savings faces mounting pressure as the target grows from £0.8m (2024/25) to £1.8m (2028/29), with no clear mechanism to achieve them. Loss of the S151 officer knowledge and lack of formal tracking creates delivery risk on savings critical to budget balance.
findings.figures: £832k target 2024/25 (62% achieved); £1.2m required 2025/26; escalating to £1.8m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The efficiency programme we have obtained is a long list of potential efficiencies to be explored which are allocated to lead officers... There are no due dates on the efficiency list and therefore it cannot be seen if savings are falling behind plan. Therefore, based on audit evidence obtained for the year ended 31 March 2025, we have concluded that there is not a formal programme in place to effectively identify, RAG rate and monitor efficiencies.

findings.headline: Regulatory enforcement action and reputational damage risk if council fails to deliver improvement plan
findings.detail: The council is required to produce an improvement plan to address all C2 weaknesses. The risk section explicitly identifies that failure to deliver could trigger regulatory enforcement action, which would indicate governance failures and damage tenant trust in the council's largest landlord service.
findings.matters: Regulatory enforcement indicates deeper governance failures and potential credit implications; failure in a major service would affect council reputation and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: 3,800+ tenant households at risk
findings.quote: If the Council does not act on the improvement areas identified in the Regulator of Social Housing's (RSH) judgement, it risks non-compliance with statutory consumer standards. This could lead to reputational damage, regulatory enforcement action, and reduced tenant trust.

findings.headline: £735k already spent on housing improvements with £191k further planned for 2026/27 to address regulatory weaknesses
findings.detail: The council has invested £735k to date on housing service improvements required to address regulatory findings. An additional £191k is planned for 2026/27. These investments must be accommodated within the Housing Revenue Account's legal requirement to remain in balance.
findings.matters: Material HRA spending on regulatory compliance reduces financial flexibility and could constrain other council borrowing or investment capacity
findings.figures: £735k spent to date; £191k planned 2026/27
findings.quote: The total to date is £735k and further investments of £191k are in plan for financial year 2026/27 whilst ensuring that the HRA remains in balance as required by the relevant legislation.

findings.headline: South Holland received a C2 regulatory grade on housing landlord services, indicating material weaknesses requiring improvement
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C2 grade following a programmed inspection from February to July 2025. A C2 grade means the regulator has identified material weaknesses likely to lead to poor tenant outcomes if not addressed. Weaknesses identified include incomplete stock condition surveys, tenant satisfaction with repairs, lack of formal tenant scrutiny mechanisms, and inconsistent approaches to vulnerable person data.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade on a major service (managing 3,800+ properties) indicates governance and service delivery weaknesses that affect council credit standing and could trigger regulatory enforcement
findings.figures: C2 grade; 3,800+ properties managed
findings.quote: C2- RSH judgement is that there are some weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and improvement is needed.

news_drafts.headline: Substantive audit procedures to verify financial statements are deferred to 2025/26, leaving the council without current audited accounts
news_drafts.lead: Lenders typically require current audited accounts to verify financial stability and borrowing capacity. Extended deferral of substantive procedures means the council cannot demonstrate its actual financial position or available borrowing headroom to…

news_drafts.headline: South Holland has received disclaimer of opinion from auditors for three consecutive financial years: 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25
news_drafts.lead: Three consecutive years without audited financial statements means the council cannot demonstrate the accuracy of its financial position, reserves, or borrowing capacity to lenders—critical information for any lending decision.

news_drafts.headline: Joint working between Council and PSPS lacks clear governance and remains a key risk area
news_drafts.lead: Unclear roles and responsibilities in shared service arrangements can lead to gaps in oversight, duplicated effort, or services not being managed according to the council's standards.
news_drafts.paper_title: IA Audit Report & Opinion 2025-26 - SHDC v3
